lines: Paints: Sky blue, Cream gold, then Pale gold.
Mix enough Cream gold for this step and steps 6 and 20; cover it between them.
Mix enough Pale gold for this step and steps 3 and 19; cover it between them.
Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint with it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
It should leave soft side-to-side bands of blue and gold, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
1.tip: The light comes from a low setting sun. The bands of Sky blue, Cream gold and Pale gold repeat, and the hills and cow will be painted over them later. Keep every stroke running side to side with a slight wave, like long thin clouds, rather than straight stripes.

lines: Let the sunset clouds and the sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
Soften the edges of this paint.
Paints, darkest first: Mountain blue, then Far violet.
Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
It should leave flat, level bands that seem to stretch away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
4.tip: Far violet makes a range with its row of peaks, and Mountain blue makes a wide band, as the after picture shows. Keep the peaks low and gentle, with no warm light on them yet; the sunset comes later.

lines: Let the far mountains and the lake, and the sunset clouds dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften the edges of this paint.
Paint: Deep green.
Mix enough Deep green for this step and steps 9 and 16; cover it between them.
Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
It should leave flat, level bands that seem to stretch away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
Leave the lighter greens from step 7 showing, as in the Result picture.
8.tip: Lay a dark strip first, then the darker bands, then the meadow. Run the hill strokes downward and the meadow strokes on a slant, and cover any sky colors still showing, as the after picture has it, so no blue or orange is left.

lines: Let the highland cow, and the hills and the meadow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften the edges of this paint.
Paint: Dark umber.
Mix enough Dark umber for this step and steps 13 and 23; cover it between them.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each bump down along its curve, and around a round shape.
It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
11.tip: Pull every stroke downward with the hair, and let some be thin, dragged strokes, as the after picture shows.

lines: Let the cow's horns and the cow's shadows dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

Brush: #4 round.
Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each bump down along its curve, and around a round shape.
It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
13.tip: Leave some of the pale Horn tan showing, as the after picture shows; it catches the light later.

lines: Let the cow and its horns, and the hills and the meadow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften the edges of this paint.
Paint: Deep green.
Brush: #6 fan. Load: A light load. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
A quick stroke upward from the base and slightly to the right, lifting off as it goes, so each mark thins at the top.
It should leave tapered marks with broken tips, denser at the base.
16.tip: Lean every mark the same way, base low and tip up and to the right, as the after picture shows, so the meadow reads as grass bending in one breeze. Space the marks apart and leave the meadow's lighter green showing between them; the picture is scattered dark dabs, not a solid dark layer.

lines: Let the meadow grass and the shaggy coat dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften the edges of this paint.
Paint: Pale gold.
Brush: 1/4 inch flat.
Press the full width of the brush down, then turn onto its edge and lighten the pressure as you pull outward, the way the hair grows.
It should leave a line that starts wide and tapers to a point.
Pale gold is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
19.tip: Pull each stroke outward, so the gold hairs stick out. Leave the ginger and honey-gold locks of the shaggy coat showing, as the after picture shows.

lines: Let the sunlit rim and the shaggy coat dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften the edges of this paint.
Paint: Dark umber.
Brush: #2 liner. Load: Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.
Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. For a tapering line, start thick and lighten as you go. Let lines fork in different directions and overlap, and wobble the edges a little.
It should leave thin, flowing lines.
Leave what steps 21 and 22 painted showing, as in the Result picture.
Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
23.tip: Paint the two nostrils first, as small commas, then the mouth line. Keep both thin so the Nose pink and the Rosy nose stay showing. The after picture also turns the nose a slightly greyer pink with a darker shadow; if yours looks too bright, a thin touch of Dark umber softened in gets you close.

Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Start with the tall upright post as one straight band, pulled downward. Then add the crossbar and the ledge as straight bars running into the post.
It should leave a flat cream frame of straight bars with clean edges, with no shading yet.
Warm white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.

lines: Let the wall and the window frame dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften this paint into the edge of the frame's shadows and the white window frame.
Paint: Warm wood brown.
Mix enough Warm wood brown for this step and step 8; cover it between them.
Brush: 1 inch flat.
Lay one long band first, then fill in the rest of the sill in long side-to-side pieces that follow its slope.
It should leave one flat, solid Warm wood brown band with no white canvas showing between the pieces.
7.tip: Run every stroke side to side along the sill's slope. The after picture also shows a slightly darker band and a thin dark lip; step 8 builds on both.

lines: Let the windowsill, and the wall and the window frame dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Soften this paint into the edge of the wooden windowsill and the frame's shadows.
Paint: Golden yellow.
Brush: 1 inch flat.
Fill it in first with long side-to-side strokes, then shape the rounded end with curved strokes.
It should leave one solid, even yellow shape with smooth rounded edges, with no wall or sill showing through.
10.tip: Make it a long, low loaf. Round its end into two stacked bulges where the blanket is folded, as the after picture shows.

lines: Let the blanket and the windowsill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Paint: Mid gray.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
Start with the big oval of the body. Then add the round head and its two pointed ears, and the curve of the back, in curved pieces like ( ), as the after picture shows.
It should leave one solid gray shape, its pieces joined with no gaps, as in the after picture.
13.tip: Give it the two pointed ears and the long, low curve of the back.

lines: Let the cat's shape and the blanket dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Brush: fan brush. Load: Thin paint. Stroke the brush on the palette until the bristles fan out.

pick.why: The step limits the streaks to the outlined band running all the way across from the top edge with its bottom about 2 in down, and Picture 3 is the only one with feathery dusky-rose and peach dry-brush streaks confined to that top band; Pictures 1 and 2 spread streaks over the whole sky, and Picture 4 shows solid peach clouds instead of broken streaks.
The step asks for faint dry-brushed peach mostly on the right-side, sun-facing ridge tops; pictures 2 and 3 show that, while 1 adds a lake that isn't asked for and 4 puts the peach on the left ridge.

The step says to paint the far mountains all the way across, with the top about 2 1/2 in and the bottom about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and only Picture 2 shows full-width bands at that height near the top; Picture 3 puts them too low, Picture 4 covers only part of the width, and Picture 1 barely adds anything.

The step says to dab small deep-green bushes all the way across the hills in loose rows that follow the existing bands, with none in the meadow; Picture 2 does this, while Picture 4 covers only the right side, Picture 1 repaints the hills themselves, and Picture 3 is a red blob.

The step says to paint all the way down to the bottom edge and fill the sky colors left between step 7's strokes so no blue or orange shows below the mountains; only Picture 2 does this, while 1 stops short of the bottom, 4 leaves sky patches, and 3 adds trees instead of dark bands.

The step says the bands must cover the whole canvas to all four edges, with the palest gold toward the low sun at the right; that rules out the half-painted 4 and the patchy 3, and only 2 has the sunny glow at the upper right, where 4's matching top shows it belongs, while 1 looks flipped.

The step puts the thin cream-gold lake at the right edge with its top about 4 1/2 in down, its left end tapering to a point; Picture 2 is the only one that does this, while Picture 3 has it at the left edge, Picture 4 leaves it short of the right edge, and Picture 1 adds hills and meadow.

The step puts the top of the green about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, has the hill bands slope down toward the lake, and leaves sky colors showing between the bands and the meadow streaks; Picture 3 fits all of this, while Picture 1 starts far too low, Picture 2 covers the lake and slopes the wrong way, and Picture 4 fills the gaps and adds a dark hill.

The step asks only for small, broken, see-through pale-gold dry-brush marks inside a 10 x 2 in band along the top edge; Picture 1 best shows a subtle lift there, Picture 3 seems to leave the top unchanged, Picture 4 spreads more solid gold well outside the band, and Picture 2 paints mountains the step never calls for.

The step says to put Dark umber along the underside of both horns, darkest at the tips, with a pale strip left along the top, and only Picture 4 does that on both horns. Picture 1 shades only one horn, Picture 2 repaints the fur instead, and Picture 3 adds extra horns.

The step asks for a flat Rust brown block-in with its left side about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, about 7 1/2 in wide, and its bottom about 2 1/2 in up with ragged points; Picture 3 matches that, while 1 is shifted right, 2 is too narrow, and 4 adds shading and detail the step doesn't call for.

The step asks for curved, downward Dark umber strokes mostly on the left side, a dark band under the fringe and low on the body, and thin dragged streaks across the rest of the coat; Picture 1 shows this, while Picture 2 stops at a hard vertical edge with no streaks on the right, Picture 3 shades outside the cow's outline, and Picture 4 paints horns instead of shading.

The step asks for both horns blocked in flat, smooth Horn tan, with the left horn bigger and sweeping up to a point and the right horn smaller, curving out and up; Picture 2 matches this, Picture 1 adds shading and dark tips, Picture 3 is missing the left horn, and Picture 4 has the sizes and placement wrong.

The step asks for tapered rust-brown locks pulled down through the whole outlined coat area, about 6 in wide by 6 1/2 in tall and including the fringe, with dark gaps left between them; Picture 1 shows that across the whole coat, while Picture 2 covers only the lower coat, Picture 3 has only a few dabs, and Picture 4 repaints the cow facing front with an extra horn.

The step calls for scattered, spaced deep-green tapered flicks leaning up and to the right, with the cow's ragged coat edge left showing; that rules out picture 4, which has light yellow-green strokes, and picture 2, which has dark marks on the cow's coat, while 1 and 3 look nearly the same and I leaned toward 3 only because its dabs seem to lean slightly more to the right.

The tip asks for most of the gold marks on the sunlit right side of the meadow with the green showing between them and the cow left alone; Picture 1 fits that, while Picture 3 keeps the gold mostly to the left, Picture 2 paints gold over the cow, and Picture 4 gilds the cow instead of the grass.

Picture 1 paints over the cow, which the step says to only soften into and leave showing, and Picture 3's marks are bright yellow and heavy rather than light, broken yellow-green flicks; between 2 and 4 I lean slightly to 2 because its marks seem to keep the up-and-right lean and sit between the dark marks, though that call is close.

The step asks only for a few thin honey-gold tapered locks on the fringe and right side of the coat plus one small meadow dab about 11 1/4 in from the left; Picture 3's dark meadow blobs and Picture 4's yellow-green coat spot break that, and Picture 1's meadow dab seems too far left.

The step only adds thin cream-gold strokes along the top curves of the two existing horns, leaving the tan undersides and dark tips; Picture 4 seems to show that lighter rim on both horns, Picture 2 looks barely changed, Picture 1 adds face detail instead, and Picture 3 adds extra horns.

The step asks for a narrow pale-gold rim mostly on the right half (top of head, fringe, down the cow's right side) with a thinner glow on the back, and Picture 1 fits that best, while Picture 2 is unchanged and Picture 3 reshapes the cow.

The step puts a pale, smoothly blended sky at the top-left corner, about 1 1/4 in wide (about 50 px) and 1 3/4 in tall (about 70 px), and Picture 2 matches that best; Picture 1 is in the wrong corner, Picture 3 is darker and streaky, and Picture 4 is too narrow.

The step calls for thin dark umber nostril commas and a mouth line on the existing nose, with the nose turning a greyer pink and a darker shadow under the mouth: pictures 3 and 4 both show this and are hard to tell apart, picture 2 is unchanged, and picture 1 paints a second nose in the wrong place.

The step asks for a flat, soft pinkish-brown muzzle centred about 7 1/4 in from the left and 8 1/2 in from the top, peeking out under the fringe with no highlight; picture 2 shows that best, picture 4 adds a white highlight, and picture 1's muzzle sits too far left.

The step places a small area about 1 in from the left edge and 1/2 in from the top (roughly 1/4 by 1 1/4 in), tapped darker over the sky, with only softening where it meets the existing sky. Picture 4 has its darker taps confined to that spot, Picture 2 spreads changes across the whole sky, Picture 3 paints at the wrong (right) side, and Picture 1 is unchanged.

The step asks for a small pale mark only on the top of the nose, at about 7 1/2 in down and 4 in from the right edge, about 1 1/4 in wide, with the rosy nose still showing around it; Picture 2's light patch fits that place and size best, while Picture 3 is in the wrong place, Picture 1 repaints the whole nose, and Picture 4's mark looks smaller than the given size.

The step only dabs a few small sunny-green dots in a 1/4 in by 1 1/4 in area near the top-left, and the tip says the result barely changes; Pictures 1, 2 and 4 look the same as the canvas before, while Picture 3 is covered in blue, which the step never asks for.

The step asks for a flat cream frame with no shading yet, sitting at the left edge, with the post taken all the way to the bottom edge; only Picture 2 does this, since Picture 1 is shaded, Picture 3 stops the post short of the bottom, and Picture 4 puts the frame on the right.

The step asks for one flat, solid brown band across the full 16 in width at the bottom, with its top about 4 1/2 in up, starting at the foot of the window frame and sloping down to the right; only picture 1 shows that, while 2 puts the sill at the top, 3 leaves gaps in the paint, and 4 stops short of the left edge.

The step says to paint the blue 'all the way across from the top edge', right up to the sky and leaves left showing at the top left, and over where the window frame will go; Picture 3 does this, Picture 4 leaves the left half bare, Picture 1 already shows the frame, and Picture 2 has the window moved to the middle.

The step says to pull each lavender-gray shadow band the full length of its bar, down the post and along the crossbar and ledge, starting from the top edge; Picture 3 does that, while Picture 2 shades only the lower part, and Pictures 1 and 4 add a windowsill or a second window the step never asks for.

The tip asks for dry-brushed shade mostly on the right side and along the front edge, with the sunlit shapes near the white frame left as plain base color and thin pale frame-shadow streaks plus a few orange streaks, and only Picture 2 shows all of that; Picture 1 puts the pattern on the wrong side, Picture 3 is a hard-edged block on the right with no streaks, and Picture 4 already lights the sunlit shapes, which is step 9.

The step places the Sunny peach patch at the canvas's left edge, about 6 1/2 in wide, as a big lower patch plus a narrow upper strip with step 8's dark bar between them; Picture 2 matches this, while Picture 1 puts it on the right, Picture 3 stops short of the full width, and Picture 4 paints the later yellow blanket instead.

The step calls for one solid, even golden-yellow low loaf about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, running off the right edge with its bottom about 1 in up and a thin strip of sill showing beneath. Picture 3 matches this, while 1 sits too high on the wall, 2 is textured and patchy with wall showing through, and 4 is a square block starting far too far right.

The step puts dark loops across the whole 14 in wide outlined blanket, thickest in the sunken middle, under the rolled top and along the fold, while leaving the sill showing; Picture 2 does this, Picture 3 paints over the sill and window, and Pictures 1 and 4 cover only part of the blanket.

The step adds small pale-yellow teardrop loops on the lit left side and roll tops of the existing blanket while leaving step 11's work showing; Picture 3 shows those added highlights, Picture 1 looks unchanged from before, Picture 2 has stray strokes outside the blanket, and Picture 4 adds the cat, which is a later step.

The step calls for one solid gray cat shape about 15 in wide, from about 1 in off the left edge to the right edge, with its top about 1 1/4 in down, a round head, two pointed ears and a low curved back, tucked into the blanket with the front roll still showing. Picture 2 matches this, while 1 is a partial shape, 3 is broken and patchy, and 4 covers the blanket's front roll.

The tip says to fill step 14's lighter gray spots, the muzzle, the two paws with thin gray lines between them, and the side patch near 9 1/4 in pulled feathery along the body; only Picture 3 does all of this, while 4 leaves the side patch unpainted, 1 puts white in the wrong places, and 2 paints stripes instead.

The step asks for one small, down-pointing rounded pink triangle where the white muzzle meets the gray face; Pictures 3 and 4 both show that and I can't tell them apart, while Picture 1 adds eyes and whiskers the step never mentions and Picture 2 scatters pink dabs across the body.

The step asks for small light-gray flicks on the head that leave the stripes showing and leave the face plain, so Picture 1 (which adds a nose) and Picture 2 (smeared paint and extra ears) fail, while Pictures 3 and 4 both show the lighter flicked head and I could not tell them apart.

graders.note: The early sky, trunks, floor and path build in believable stages. In the middle the lesson makes big jumps and pictures that don't match the paints. Step 9 turns a bare floor into a full leaf carpet, bushes and a green bush from a grey-brown 'Moss green'. Step 4 gives the firs red trunks that no paint covers. Step 11's greyish Pale gold shows up as bright yellow. Step 13 fully models the rock from one dark dry-brush. Step 15 repaints the background trunks as sharp birches, and its own tip admits it. Step 17 turns flat grey trunks into finished, textured birches with highlights from a single dark bark paint.

The window view breaks early. Steps 2 and 3 name leaf greens, but their pictures show only deeper blue and then no change at all. The green and yellow leaves appear by magic in step 4's wall-blue step, along with a ghost of the frame post. Step 8 shades with the very same brown as the base yet its picture adds pale streaks and sunlit shapes. Step 14's Dark gray is almost the same color as Mid gray, while its picture models the whole cat and its tip contradicts the outlined box. Step 11 jumps from flat yellow to a fully formed knit blanket, step 18's 'Light gray' is darker than the grays under it, and step 20's picture already shows the whiskers meant for step 21. The flat block-ins of the sill, blanket and cat, plus the white patches, pink, nose and whiskers, are clear and paintable.

The window view goes wrong first. Steps 2 and 3 name greens, but their pictures show only bluer sky, and step 3's picture doesn't change at all. Then green and yellow leaves suddenly appear in step 4, which names only wall blues, and step 4's picture already has a faint ghost of the window post. Several steps name a paint that can't make their picture: step 8 shades the sill with its own base brown, and step 14's 'Dark gray' is almost the same as the mid gray yet the picture models the whole cat. Step 18's 'Light gray' mixes darker than the base, and step 16 names only charcoal while its picture also lightens and textures the whole coat, a big jump done by magic. The sill, blanket block-in, white patches, ears and face steps are sound and look like a real painting in progress.

The order (sky, far woods, floor, leaves, rock, birches, lights) is sound, but several pictures show more than their words and paints can make. Step 4's firs arrive finished with red-brown trunks from two greens. Step 9 covers the whole bottom half, plus bushes and treetop leaves, with a multicolored mosaic in one step. Steps 13, 15 and 17 also show things no instruction covers: stone highlights on the rock, middle birches redrawn (step 15 even tells the painter to ignore this), and the chalky gray trunks of step 16 suddenly turning clean white. Paint colors often disagree with what the pictures show: gray Smoky brown pulls red trunks, brownish Moss green appears olive, and Birch white is darker than the whites it is meant to brighten.

The sky, mountains, bushes, horns and grass flicks build up well, but several pictures show more than their paints can make. Step 7 leaves odd mask-like holes and drips. Step 8 names only Deep green yet jumps to a finished, wind-streaked meadow full of yellow greens. Step 14 pulls 'ginger locks' in Rust brown, the cow's own base colour, but the picture shows bright orange locks, a formed fringe and a face. Smaller mismatches: step 11's dark-only shading also lightens and textures the whole coat. Step 20's outline is 1/4 in square, though it covers both horns. Step 22's 'Nose pink' is an olive grey that paints as a white patch. Step 23 says to line the nostrils but regreys the whole nose and face.

The sky, mountains, bushes, flat cow block-in, horns and grass flicks are believable and paintable. Several pictures don't match their paints. In step 14, Rust brown over a Rust brown base somehow makes light orange-tan locks with dark gaps. Step 22's 'Nose pink' is mixed as an olive grey-green (#777a4d), yet it shows as a pale streak. Step 23 recolours the whole nose and firms up the muzzle and fringe, and its tip admits it. Step 7's hard-edged green blotches with sky showing through the holes are patches no brush makes. Step 8 then jumps from those blotches to a finished-looking lit meadow using one dark green. From step 11 to step 20 the cow reads as seen from behind, and the face only arrives with the nose steps.
